# Week 6, Day 2.1 - Prerequisites check

**No new TypeScript today.** Today is a design argument, not a language lesson - so this file is
short on purpose.

| In play | Taught in |
|---|---|
| Classes, `readonly` fields | [week3/day3_1](/learn/w3/d3/p1) |
| `abstract`, `extends`, `protected` | [week5/day3_1](/learn/w5/d3/p1) |
| Typed parameters, default parameters | [week3/day3_1](/learn/w3/d3/p1) |
| `test.beforeEach` | [week3/day2_2](/learn/w3/d2/p2) |
| Importing across folders | [week5/day4_1](/learn/w5/d4/p1) |

One small thing *is* new, below.

**Next:** [Day 2.2 - What a page object may assert](/learn/w6/d2/p2)

## The one new thing - a shared literal, exported

Today a page class asserts a fixed message. Both the class and the test may want that string, so
it is exported as a `const` beside the class rather than typed twice:

```ts
export const WRONG_CREDENTIALS = "Login and/or password are wrong.";
```

One definition, two importers, and the compiler catches a typo in either. The alternative -
the sentence written out in both files - is the same duplication problem as a locator in two
places, in prose form.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

`false` on that last line, from one capital letter. That is why it is exported once.

**Next:** [Day 2.2 - What a page object may assert](/learn/w6/d2/p2)

blocks.text:
# Week 6, Day 2.2 - What a page object may assert

[Week 5 Day 3](/learn/w5/d3/p2) gave you a rule: **no `expect()` inside a page object.**
Today that rule gets its exception, and the exception has a sharp edge.

> **Mode: test-runner.** This part is about running specs with the Playwright test runner. The studio editor runs library code, so follow these along in your own checkout.

## Step 1 - the rule, and the one case it excludes

| The assertion is about | Belongs in | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Whatever *this test* sent or expects | the **test** | only the test knows it |
| A message the page **always** shows | the **page class** | it is a fact about the screen |

"Login and/or password are wrong." is the same sentence for every wrong credential ever typed.
It is not test data - it is a property of the login page. So it lives there.

The sharp edge: **"invariant" has to be proved, not assumed.** Step 2 proves it.

Step 2 of that run sends three different wrong credentials - `("a","b")`, `("","")`,
`("username","nope")` - and gets **one** message. That is what earns `assertRefused()` its place
in the class.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## Step 2 - the app's real behaviour, which the session got wrong

The session signs in with `username` / `password` and demonstrates a "bypass": when the browser
shows an SSL warning, type the inner URL directly.

Neither works any more. Probed, not assumed:

| Attempt | Result |
|---|---|
| `POST /signin.html` over HTTP with those credentials | **302 → `login.html?login_error=true`** |
| `https://zero.webappsecurity.com` | `ERR_SSL_VERSION_OR_CIPHER_MISMATCH` |
| Same, with `ignoreHTTPSErrors: true` | still fails - that flag ignores *certificates*, not ciphers |
| Navigating straight to `/bank/account-summary.html` | redirects to `/login.html` - there **is** a guard |

So the bypass trick cannot work: there is nothing to bypass *to*. Step 3 of the spec asserts the
refusal, which keeps the finding true rather than leaving a broken lesson behind.

**The transferable skill is the diagnosis.** A cipher mismatch is not a cert error, so
`ignoreHTTPSErrors` never fixes it; and a redirect to `/login.html` tells you a guard exists
before you spend an hour on the login form.

`ERR_SSL_VERSION_OR_CIPHER_MISMATCH` **despite** `ignoreHTTPSErrors: true`, and
`login.html?login_error=true` from the documented credentials. Two independent dead ends, so the
signed-in half of this app is genuinely out of reach - not a wait or a flag away.

## Step 3 - fill and submit: one method or two?

The session writes login as **one** method and feedback as **two**. That is not inconsistency.

| Screen | Buttons after typing | Methods |
|---|---|---|
| Login | 1 (Sign in) | `login()` - fill **and** submit |
| Feedback | 2 (Send, Clear) | `fillForm()`, then `submitForm()` **or** `resetForm()` |

The rule: **split when the screen offers a choice.** Had `fillForm()` ended with a click, the
"clear the form" test could not exist at all - one method would have decided for every test that
will ever use it.

Steps 4 and 5 of the run are that pair: identical fill, opposite endings.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## Step 4 - visibility versus text

`assertSent()` checks the heading is **visible**. It does not check what it says - because the
confirmation is personalised:

```
Thank you for your comments, Leela.
```

The name came from the test. So the test asserts the sentence; the page asserts that a heading
appeared. Step 6 of the run does exactly that, one line each.

| Assertion | Owner |
|---|---|
| `expect(feedbackTitle).toBeVisible()` | page class - always true after sending |
| `toContainText("Thank you for your comments, Leela.")` | test - it chose "Leela" |

## Step 5 - the anti-pattern

Step 7 of the run is deliberately wrong:

```ts
const searchBoxDeclaredHere = page.locator("#searchTerm");   // in the TEST
```

It **passes**, which is what makes it dangerous. When that id changes, the failure is in a test
file and no page class mentions the selector - so the hunt starts in the wrong place, and every
test that copied the line has to be found.

> One locator in one test is not a disaster. It is the precedent that is: the next person copies
> the nearest example.

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | Consequence |
|---|---|
| Asserting test-specific text in the class | the class serves one test and blocks the rest |
| Assuming a message is invariant | Step 2 exists to check; do it before moving the assertion in |
| `ignoreHTTPSErrors` for a cipher error | it cannot help; you lose an hour before reading the error code |
| One combined method on a two-button screen | half the tests you need become unwritable |

**Next:** [Day 2.3 - Journeys, and a visual check inside a page object](/learn/w6/d2/p3)

# Week 6, Day 2.3 - Journeys, and a visual check inside a page object

Same page objects, composed into flows - and one more thing a page class may own.

> **Mode: test-runner.** This part is about running specs with the Playwright test runner. The studio editor runs library code, so follow these along in your own checkout.

## Preconditions belong in `beforeEach`

A fund-transfer test needs: land on the site, sign in, navigate to the right tab, *then* the
thing being tested. Only the last part is the test.

| Line | Is it the test? |
|---|---|
| `homePage.visit()` | no - precondition |
| `loginPage.signIn()` | no - precondition |
| `navBar.clickOnTab("Add Payee")` | usually no |
| `expect(...)` | **yes** |

Everything answering "no" goes in `beforeEach`, so each test body is only its own claim.

Look at the imports in that file:

```ts
import { LoginPage as BankLoginPage } from "../../week5/generated/pages/LoginPage";
import { DashboardPage } from "../../week5/generated/pages/DashboardPage";
```

**Week 5's classes, reused - not rewritten.** That is most of what a page-object library is for.
`as BankLoginPage` renames on import, because week 6 has a `LoginPage` of its own for a different
site and two things called `LoginPage` in one file would be unreadable.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

| Detail | Value |
|---|---|
| Baseline written to | `day2-visual.visualdemo.ts-snapshots/zero-login-error-win32.png` |
| `-win32` suffix | baselines are platform-locked - [week4/day5_2](/learn/w4/d5/p2) |
| File named `.visualdemo.ts` | keeps the root `testMatch` from collecting it |
| Step 1 asserts visibility first | `toHaveScreenshot` on a missing element gives a timeout, which reads like a visual diff and is not one |

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## So what may a page class own?

| Owns | Example |
|---|---|
| Locators | `errorBanner` |
| Actions named for people | `login()`, `resetForm()` |
| **Invariant** assertions | `assertRefused()`, `assertReset()` |
| A visual baseline for its own chrome | `snapshotErrorBanner()` |
| Nothing that varies per test | not the name a test typed, not a row count it chose |

## POM and externalised locators

[Week 5 Day 5.3](/learn/w5/d5/p3) weighed moving selectors into JSON and concluded a page
class already gives you one-place-to-edit, plus autocomplete and a compiler. The session reaches
the same verdict from the other direction: *with page objects you do not externalise, because the
page object already is the one place.* Doing both means two.

**Next:** [Day 2.4 - Practice](/learn/w6/d2/p4)

problems.statement:
**Prove an invariant yourself**
Pick a message on Zero Bank you think is invariant. Send at least three different inputs and
compare what comes back.

**Right when:** you can say *proved* or *disproved*, with the three outputs - and you moved the
assertion into the page class only if it passed.

**Break rule 3 the tempting way**
Add `expect(this.feedbackTitle).toContainText("Thank you for your comments, Leela.")` inside
`assertSent()` in a copy of `FeedbackPage`. Then write a test that submits as "Katy".

**Right when:** the second test fails, and you can explain why in one sentence about ownership.

**Combine what should be split**
In a copy of `FeedbackPage`, make `fillForm()` end with a click on Send. Now try to write the
"clear the form" test.

**Right when:** you can state precisely why it is now impossible without a second method.

**Reproduce the SSL diagnosis**
Navigate to `https://zero.webappsecurity.com/login.html`, once plainly and once with
`ignoreHTTPSErrors: true`.

**Right when:** you get the same error both times and can say why that flag is the wrong tool -
and what error a genuine certificate problem would have given instead.

**Find the guard**
Navigate straight to `/bank/account-summary.html` in a fresh context and follow what happens.

**Right when:** you can name the final URL and say what it tells you about the app before you
have looked at the login form at all.

**A journey with a precondition**
Write a spec whose `beforeEach` reaches the Zero Bank feedback form *through* the home page, then
three tests: send, clear, and send-with-empty-fields.

**Right when:** no test body contains a `visit()` or a `click` on the feedback link, and you can
say what the empty-fields case actually does (find out - do not guess).

**A visual baseline of your own**
Add a `snapshotForm()` method to a copy of `FeedbackPage` and run it twice under
`day2-visual.config.ts`.

**Right when:** run one fails writing the baseline, run two passes, and you can point at the file
it wrote and explain the `-win32` in its name.

**Hunt the anti-pattern**
Search the specs you have written across weeks 5 and 6 for locators declared at test level.

> Hint: `npx playwright test --list` will not find these. Try grepping for `page.locator(` and
> `getBy` inside your spec files.

**Right when:** you have a count, and for each one either a page class to move it into or a
reason it genuinely belongs where it is.
